seo.title: Key Terms in Distributed Systems: The Definitive Glossary
seo.description: Follow one system-design interview from a vague multi-leader proposal through the exact anomalies, isolation levels, replication models, shard-key choices, and consensus rules that make the design defensible.

content.markdown:
## Stage 1 — How Vocabulary Breaks System Design Interviews (and Production Systems)

You are 35 minutes into a system design interview. You have just proposed multi-leader replication for a globally distributed social feed. The interviewer pauses and says: "Your design doesn't account for write skew. Walk me through how you'd prevent it."

A nod is not an answer. Write skew is a specific interleaving: two transactions each read an overlapping predicate, each decides the constraint still holds, and each writes a **different** row. No single-row lock fires. Both commits succeed. The predicate the product promised — at least one doctor on call, one seat left, one canonical post id — is now false.

That is different from a dirty read (you saw an uncommitted write that later vanished), a lost update (two read-modify-writes hit the **same** row and one overwrote the other), and "eventual consistency" (replicas have not caught up yet). If the answer uses those phrases interchangeably, the interviewer cannot tell which mechanism you would actually ship.

The decision in this stage is to freeze the design and name the anomaly before picking a database feature. The component that must change is the candidate's next sentence, not the diagram. The observable output is a sentence of the form: "Two writers can each pass the on-call check and update different rows; I will close that with Serializable isolation or a shared lock row, not with multi-leader replication."

The same failure shows up in production incident reviews. A ticket titled "inconsistent data" hides three different bugs and three different fixes. Vocabulary is the routing key for the rest of this scenario.

## Stage 2 — Consistency Anomalies: The Ways Transactions Can Lie to You

Once the anomaly has a name, classify it against the catalog. Each row below is a different lie the database can tell a transaction, and each lie has a different business symptom.

| Anomaly | What the transaction observes | What the product ships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dirty read | A value that another transaction has not committed and may roll back | A decision based on state that never existed |
| Non-repeatable read | Two selects of the same row in one transaction return different committed values | A branch taken on a number that is already stale |
| Phantom read | A range query grows or shrinks inside one transaction | A constraint check that passed on an incomplete set |
| Read skew | Two related rows are read from different points in time | A transfer that looks balanced in neither account |
| Write skew | Two transactions each pass a shared check and write non-overlapping rows | Double booking, empty on-call roster |
| Lost update | Two read-modify-writes of the same row; one write disappears | A balance incremented once instead of twice |
| Dirty write | A second transaction overwrites an uncommitted first write | A row whose history cannot be reconstructed |

The on-call example is write skew, not a lost update. Alice reads `count(on_call) = 2` and sets her own row to off. Bob does the same for his row. Neither update touches the other's row, so Read Committed and snapshot isolation both allow both commits. A later `count(on_call)` returns 0.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alice
    participant DB
    participant Bob
    Alice->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Bob->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Alice->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Alice: 2
    Bob->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Bob: 2
    Alice->>DB: set Alice off
    Bob->>DB: set Bob off
    Alice->>DB: COMMIT
    Bob->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over DB: Invariant broken: zero doctors on call
```

The decision is to pick one row from that table and refuse the others. The component behavior is the interleaving above. The observable output is a query after both commits that shows the invariant false — proof you named the right anomaly.

## Stage 3 — Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL's Six-Way Dial Between Safety and Speed

Isolation is the dial that decides which rows from the previous table are still possible. PostgreSQL does not implement Read Uncommitted; that setting is promoted to Read Committed. The levels you actually choose among are Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable.

Read Committed takes a **new snapshot per statement**. Two selects of `balance` inside one transaction can return 100 and then 50 if another transaction committed in between. That is a non-repeatable read. It is the default, and it is the right default for single-statement work. It does not protect check-then-act logic.

Repeatable Read takes **one snapshot for the transaction**. The same row keeps the same value, and PostgreSQL's MVCC visibility rules also hide phantoms that were inserted after the snapshot. It still allows write skew, because each transaction's snapshot cannot see the other transaction's concurrent write to a different row.

Serializable in PostgreSQL is serializable snapshot isolation. Transactions still run on snapshots, but the engine records read-write dependencies. When Alice's read depends on a row Bob writes and Bob's read depends on a row Alice writes, one commit is aborted with `SQLSTATE 40001`. The survivor stays. The aborted session must retry; on retry it sees the updated count and refuses to go off call.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call
  WHERE shift = current_date AND status = 'active';
-- application: proceed only when count > 1
UPDATE on_call
   SET status = 'off'
 WHERE doctor_id = $1 AND shift = current_date;
COMMIT;
```

The decision is not "turn Serializable on for the whole pool." Ordinary single-row updates stay at Read Committed, often with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the row they will change. Only the multi-row predicate — on-call count, remaining seats across a cabin, inventory across warehouses — moves to Serializable, and the service retries `40001` with backoff.

Oracle's label "Serializable" is snapshot isolation. It does not give you this abort. If the design says "we set serializable," the observable output must name the engine: a PostgreSQL `40001` in the logs, or an explicit lock row if the engine cannot detect the cycle.

## Stage 4 — Replication Models and the Consistency Spectrum Across Databases

Isolation answers what one node lets concurrent transactions see. Replication answers what **another node** is allowed to serve after the client was told the write succeeded.

Single-leader replication gives one node the right to order writes and ships that log to followers. Synchronous replication waits until a configured set of followers has the record before the leader acks the client. A failover then has the write. Asynchronous replication acks from the leader alone. It is faster, and a crash can drop the tail that followers never received. Readers on a lagging follower can also miss the write; that is replica lag, not write skew.

Multi-leader replication lets more than one node accept writes, usually one leader per region. Conflicts are inevitable when the same key is written in two places. Last-write-wins is a policy for discarding one of them, not a proof that both happened. Use it only when the product can say which value may disappear.

Leaderless replication (the Dynamo family) lets any replica accept a write and reconciles with quorums and read repair. A write quorum `W` and a read quorum `R` with `W + R > N` overlap, so a read sees the latest write if no node is missing from both sets. If `W + R ≤ N`, a read can miss a write that succeeded. That is a different knob from isolation level, and interview answers that mix them are answering two questions with one word.

The decision for the social feed's authoritative post record is single-leader synchronous replication (or a quorum that overlaps reads and writes). Multi-leader is allowed only for data whose conflict rule is written down. The observable output is: after the client sees success, a promoted follower or a quorum read returns the new post, and replication lag is a separate metric from serialization failures.

## Stage 5 — Partitioning and Sharding: Distributing Data Across Nodes

Replication copies the **same** data so you can survive a node loss and spread reads. Sharding splits the data so no single node holds every row or absorbs every write. The shard key is the column the router uses to choose a node. It is expensive to change later because every row may have to move.

A useful key has high cardinality, spreads writes, matches the query you run most often, and does not change for the life of the row. `user_id` on a timeline does that: one user's posts live together, and writes from many users spread out. `created_at` looks high-cardinality and still sends every insert to the newest shard. `country_code` is easy to explain and creates a permanent hot shard for the largest country.

Range sharding keeps order, so a between-query can stay on one shard, and it creates a hot tail when keys increase monotonically. Hash sharding spreads sequential keys and turns every range scan into a scatter-gather. Consistent hashing keeps most keys in place when you add a node: about `1/N` of the data moves, especially with virtual nodes. A directory (shard map) lets you place a celebrity key on its own node, and the map itself becomes a dependency that must stay available.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Client --> Router
  Router -->|user_id hash| S0[Shard 0]
  Router -->|user_id hash| S1[Shard 1]
  Router -->|no shard key| Fanout[Scatter-gather]
  Fanout --> S0
  Fanout --> S1
```

The decision is to shard the feed by `user_id` (or a compound tenant plus user key) with hashing or consistent hashing, and to serve "latest across everyone" from a separate index rather than from a scatter on the primary table. The observable output is a timeline read that touches one shard, plus a dashboard query whose plan shows N shard round-trips if someone forgot the key.

## Stage 6 — Consensus and Leader Election: Deciding Who Gets the Final Say

Sharding and replication both assume someone knows which node is the leader and which shard owns a key. If two nodes both believe they are leader, you get two histories. Clocks do not settle that argument: "latest timestamp" is another last-write-wins policy, and clocks drift.

Consensus protocols (Raft is the one most teams can walk through) elect one leader per term and replicate a log. A candidate needs votes from a majority. A log entry is committed only after a majority has stored it. A partition that holds only a minority cannot elect a leader and cannot commit. Clients in that partition see errors and retry. That unavailability is the mechanism that prevents split brain.

The same rule applies to the shard map. If the map is updated by a single node without a quorum, a stale router can send writes to a shard that no longer owns the key. Leader election for the database and quorum agreement for the map are the same idea: a majority must agree before the configuration is real.

Do not implement "whoever heartbeats last wins" in application code. The decision is to put leader election and the shard map on a consensus system (the database's own Raft group, or a dedicated one) and to surface the term and commit index. The observable output is one leader per term, a commit index that does not move backwards, and a minority partition that rejects writes instead of accepting a second log.

## Key learnings

- Name the anomaly before you name the feature. Write skew, lost update, replica lag, and split brain are four different bugs.
- Read Committed and Repeatable Read do not close write skew. PostgreSQL Serializable does, and the application must retry `40001`.
- Replication chooses who may ack a write. Sharding chooses which node stores it. Consensus chooses who is allowed to decide either of those facts.
- A shard key is a query-locality decision. A monotonic key with range sharding creates a hot shard no amount of replication will fix.
- A minority partition that still accepts writes has already forked history. Quorum refusal is the correct degraded mode.

footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

footerPosts.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

footerPosts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
footerPosts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
footerPosts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI

An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

morePosts.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
morePosts.subtitle: Trade exact answers for fixed memory and O(1) operations: a comparative guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch.
morePosts.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

morePosts.subtitle: A beginner-friendly way to structure requirements, estimates, diagrams, and trade-offs in your first design round.

morePosts.title: Elasticsearch vs Time-Series DB: Key Differences Explained
morePosts.subtitle: Should you store logs in Elasticsearch or InfluxDB? We compare Search Engines vs. Time-Series DBs
morePosts.brief: Elasticsearch is built for **search** — full-text log queries, fuzzy matching, and relevance ranking via an inverted index. InfluxDB and Prometheus are built for **metrics** — numeric time series with aggressive compression. Picking the wrong one wastes 10× the storage or makes queries 100× slower.

morePosts.subtitle: Learn how to choose entities, indexes, and schema evolution strategies that match real query patterns at scale.
morePosts.brief: In system design interviews, data modeling is where architecture meets reality. A good model starts from query patterns, chooses clear entity boundaries, defines indexes deliberately, and includes a schema evolution path so the system can change without breaking reads and writes.

morePosts.title: System Design Replication and Failover: Keep Services Alive When a Primary Dies
morePosts.subtitle: A clear guide to replicas, failover detection, replica lag, and the trade-offs behind reliable database designs.
morePosts.brief: Replication means keeping multiple copies of your data so the system can survive machine, process, or availability-zone failures. Failover is the coordinated act of promoting a healthy replica, rerouting traffic, and recovering without corrupting data.

Once the anomaly has a name, classify it against the catalog. Each row below is a different lie the database can tell a transaction, and each lie has a different business symptom.

| Anomaly | What the transaction observes | What the product ships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dirty read | A value that another transaction has not committed and may roll back | A decision based on state that never existed |
| Non-repeatable read | Two selects of the same row in one transaction return different committed values | A branch taken on a number that is already stale |
| Phantom read | A range query grows or shrinks inside one transaction | A constraint check that passed on an incomplete set |
| Read skew | Two related rows are read from different points in time | A transfer that looks balanced in neither account |
| Write skew | Two transactions each pass a shared check and write non-overlapping rows | Double booking, empty on-call roster |
| Lost update | Two read-modify-writes of the same row; one write disappears | A balance incremented once instead of twice |
| Dirty write | A second transaction overwrites an uncommitted first write | A row whose history cannot be reconstructed |

The on-call example is write skew, not a lost update. Alice reads `count(on_call) = 2` and sets her own row to off. Bob does the same for his row. Neither update touches the other's row, so Read Committed and snapshot isolation both allow both commits. A later `count(on_call)` returns 0.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alice
    participant DB
    participant Bob
    Alice->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Bob->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Alice->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Alice: 2
    Bob->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Bob: 2
    Alice->>DB: set Alice off
    Bob->>DB: set Bob off
    Alice->>DB: COMMIT
    Bob->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over DB: Invariant broken: zero doctors on call
```

The decision is to pick one row from that table and refuse the others. The component behavior is the interleaving above. The observable output is a query after both commits that shows the invariant false — proof you named the right anomaly.

## Stage 3 — Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL's Six-Way Dial Between Safety and Speed

Isolation is the dial that decides which rows from the previous table are still possible. PostgreSQL does not implement Read Uncommitted; that setting is promoted to Read Committed. The levels you actually choose among are Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable.

Read Committed takes a **new snapshot per statement**. Two selects of `balance` inside one transaction can return 100 and then 50 if another transaction committed in between. That is a non-repeatable read. It is the default, and it is the right default for single-statement work. It does not protect check-then-act logic.

Repeatable Read takes **one snapshot for the transaction**. The same row keeps the same value, and PostgreSQL's MVCC visibility rules also hide phantoms that were inserted after the snapshot. It still allows write skew, because each transaction's snapshot cannot see the other transaction's concurrent write to a different row.

Serializable in PostgreSQL is serializable snapshot isolation. Transactions still run on snapshots, but the engine records read-write dependencies. When Alice's read depends on a row Bob writes and Bob's read depends on a row Alice writes, one commit is aborted with `SQLSTATE 40001`. The survivor stays. The aborted session must retry; on retry it sees the updated count and refuses to go off call.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call
  WHERE shift = current_date AND status = 'active';
-- application: proceed only when count > 1
UPDATE on_call
   SET status = 'off'
 WHERE doctor_id = $1 AND shift = current_date;
COMMIT;
```

The decision is not "turn Serializable on for the whole pool." Ordinary single-row updates stay at Read Committed, often with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the row they will change. Only the multi-row predicate — on-call count, remaining seats across a cabin, inventory across warehouses — moves to Serializable, and the service retries `40001` with backoff.

Oracle's label "Serializable" is snapshot isolation. It does not give you this abort. If the design says "we set serializable," the observable output must name the engine: a PostgreSQL `40001` in the logs, or an explicit lock row if the engine cannot detect the cycle.

## Stage 4 — Replication Models and the Consistency Spectrum Across Databases

Isolation answers what one node lets concurrent transactions see. Replication answers what **another node** is allowed to serve after the client was told the write succeeded.

Single-leader replication gives one node the right to order writes and ships that log to followers. Synchronous replication waits until a configured set of followers has the record before the leader acks the client. A failover then has the write. Asynchronous replication acks from the leader alone. It is faster, and a crash can drop the tail that followers never received. Readers on a lagging follower can also miss the write; that is replica lag, not write skew.

Multi-leader replication lets more than one node accept writes, usually one leader per region. Conflicts are inevitable when the same key is written in two places. Last-write-wins is a policy for discarding one of them, not a proof that both happened. Use it only when the product can say which value may disappear.

Leaderless replication (the Dynamo family) lets any replica accept a write and reconciles with quorums and read repair. A write quorum `W` and a read quorum `R` with `W + R > N` overlap, so a read sees the latest write if no node is missing from both sets. If `W + R ≤ N`, a read can miss a write that succeeded. That is a different knob from isolation level, and interview answers that mix them are answering two questions with one word.

The decision for the social feed's authoritative post record is single-leader synchronous replication (or a quorum that overlaps reads and writes). Multi-leader is allowed only for data whose conflict rule is written down. The observable output is: after the client sees success, a promoted follower or a quorum read returns the new post, and replication lag is a separate metric from serialization failures.

## Stage 5 — Partitioning and Sharding: Distributing Data Across Nodes

Replication copies the **same** data so you can survive a node loss and spread reads. Sharding splits the data so no single node holds every row or absorbs every write. The shard key is the column the router uses to choose a node. It is expensive to change later because every row may have to move.

A useful key has high cardinality, spreads writes, matches the query you run most often, and does not change for the life of the row. `user_id` on a timeline does that: one user's posts live together, and writes from many users spread out. `created_at` looks high-cardinality and still sends every insert to the newest shard. `country_code` is easy to explain and creates a permanent hot shard for the largest country.

Range sharding keeps order, so a between-query can stay on one shard, and it creates a hot tail when keys increase monotonically. Hash sharding spreads sequential keys and turns every range scan into a scatter-gather. Consistent hashing keeps most keys in place when you add a node: about `1/N` of the data moves, especially with virtual nodes. A directory (shard map) lets you place a celebrity key on its own node, and the map itself becomes a dependency that must stay available.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Client --> Router
  Router -->|user_id hash| S0[Shard 0]
  Router -->|user_id hash| S1[Shard 1]
  Router -->|no shard key| Fanout[Scatter-gather]
  Fanout --> S0
  Fanout --> S1
```

The decision is to shard the feed by `user_id` (or a compound tenant plus user key) with hashing or consistent hashing, and to serve "latest across everyone" from a separate index rather than from a scatter on the primary table. The observable output is a timeline read that touches one shard, plus a dashboard query whose plan shows N shard round-trips if someone forgot the key.

## Stage 6 — Consensus and Leader Election: Deciding Who Gets the Final Say

Sharding and replication both assume someone knows which node is the leader and which shard owns a key. If two nodes both believe they are leader, you get two histories. Clocks do not settle that argument: "latest timestamp" is another last-write-wins policy, and clocks drift.

Consensus protocols (Raft is the one most teams can walk through) elect one leader per term and replicate a log. A candidate needs votes from a majority. A log entry is committed only after a majority has stored it. A partition that holds only a minority cannot elect a leader and cannot commit. Clients in that partition see errors and retry. That unavailability is the mechanism that prevents split brain.

The same rule applies to the shard map. If the map is updated by a single node without a quorum, a stale router can send writes to a shard that no longer owns the key. Leader election for the database and quorum agreement for the map are the same idea: a majority must agree before the configuration is real.

Do not implement "whoever heartbeats last wins" in application code. The decision is to put leader election and the shard map on a consensus system (the database's own Raft group, or a dedicated one) and to surface the term and commit index. The observable output is one leader per term, a commit index that does not move backwards, and a minority partition that rejects writes instead of accepting a second log.

## Key learnings

- Name the anomaly before you name the feature. Write skew, lost update, replica lag, and split brain are four different bugs.
- Read Committed and Repeatable Read do not close write skew. PostgreSQL Serializable does, and the application must retry `40001`.
- Replication chooses who may ack a write. Sharding chooses which node stores it. Consensus chooses who is allowed to decide either of those facts.
- A shard key is a query-locality decision. A monotonic key with range sharding creates a hot shard no amount of replication will fix.
- A minority partition that still accepts writes has already forked history. Quorum refusal is the correct degraded mode.

stages.decisionOrAction: Stop the multi-leader feed design and name the exact anomaly the interviewer asked about: write skew, not a generic consistency problem.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Forces the high-level design to use one term per failure mode so the rest of the interview can be traced to a mechanism.

stages.componentBehavior: The interviewer pauses after the multi-leader proposal and asks how the design prevents write skew. The candidate must restate the invariant (two writers each pass a shared check, then write non-overlapping rows) before choosing a control.
stages.observableOutput: The answer names write skew, distinguishes it from dirty reads and lost updates, and commits to a concrete control (serializable isolation or an explicit lock row) instead of saying the system will be eventually consistent.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Consistency Anomalies: The Ways Transactions Can Lie to You
stages.decisionOrAction: Classify the feed bug as one anomaly from the standard set: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, read skew, write skew, lost update, or dirty write.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Supplies the anomaly catalog the design must rule in or out before isolation is chosen.

stages.componentBehavior: Two concurrent sessions read the same on-call or inventory predicate, each concludes the constraint still holds, and each writes a different row. Neither statement conflicts at the row lock, so both commits succeed and the predicate is false.
stages.observableOutput: A post-commit query shows the invariant broken (zero doctors on call, or two bookings of one seat) even though each transaction's own reads looked correct.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL's Six-Way Dial Between Safety and Speed
stages.decisionOrAction: Raise only the transactions that check a multi-row invariant to Serializable, and keep ordinary single-row updates at Read Committed with row locks.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Maps ANSI labels to PostgreSQL mechanisms: statement snapshots, transaction snapshots, and serializable snapshot isolation.

stages.componentBehavior: Read Committed gives each statement a fresh snapshot, so two selects in one transaction can disagree. Repeatable Read freezes the snapshot but still allows write skew. Serializable tracks read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001.
stages.observableOutput: The on-call update either commits alone or the second session retries after 40001 and then sees that the last on-call doctor is already off, so it refuses the second checkout.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Replication Models and the Consistency Spectrum Across Databases
stages.decisionOrAction: Choose single-leader synchronous replication for the feed's authoritative writes, and treat multi-leader as an explicit conflict-resolution design rather than a latency shortcut.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Defines who accepts writes and which replicas must acknowledge them before the client is told the write succeeded.

stages.componentBehavior: A single leader orders writes and ships the log. Synchronous followers block the ack until a quorum has the record. Asynchronous followers return early and can lose the tail on failover. Multi-leader and leaderless modes accept writes on more than one node and must reconcile divergent versions.
stages.observableOutput: After the client receives a success, a failover or a read from another replica still returns the new post, or the design documents the window where a replica can lag or diverge.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Partitioning and Sharding: Distributing Data Across Nodes
stages.decisionOrAction: Shard the feed by a high-cardinality immutable key that matches the dominant query, and refuse a timestamp or auto-increment key that piles every new write onto one shard.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Decides which node owns a row and which queries stay local versus scatter-gather.

stages.componentBehavior: The router hashes or ranges the shard key and sends the write to one shard. Queries that include the key hit one node. Queries that omit it fan out, wait for the slowest shard, and merge. Changing the shard count with modulo hashing moves almost every row; consistent hashing moves about 1/N.

stages.title: Stage 6 — Consensus and Leader Election: Deciding Who Gets the Final Say
stages.decisionOrAction: Use a consensus protocol for the shard map and the replication leader, and do not let application nodes elect a leader with a single timeout and a last-write-wins clock.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Requires a quorum to agree on one leader and one log order before a configuration or write is committed.

stages.componentBehavior: Followers vote in a term. A candidate becomes leader only with a majority. The leader replicates log entries and commits them once a majority has stored them. A partitioned minority cannot commit, which prevents split brain at the cost of unavailability.
stages.observableOutput: Operators see one leader per term, committed log indexes that never go backwards, and a minority partition that rejects writes instead of accepting a second history.

outcome.endToEndResult: The same vocabulary now drives both the interview answer and the production controls: name the anomaly, pick the isolation or replication rule that closes it, place data with a shard key that matches the query, and elect one leader with a quorum.
outcome.observedUserBehavior: Readers and writers see either a committed post that survives failover or an explicit retry, never a silent double-booking or a second history.
outcome.observedOperatorBehavior: Dashboards show isolation aborts, replication lag, hot shards, and leader terms as separate signals instead of one 'consistency' alert.
keyTradeoffs: Serializable closes write skew but requires retry handling for SQLSTATE 40001.
Synchronous replication removes the lost-tail window and adds ack latency.
A query-aligned shard key makes the primary path local and pushes secondary access patterns onto indexes.
Quorum consensus prevents split brain and refuses writes when a majority is unreachable.

alternatives.title: Stay on Read Committed and lock the predicate
alternatives.explanation: For a single hot row, SELECT FOR UPDATE is enough and avoids serialization retries. It does not close write skew across two different rows unless you also lock a shared sentinel row.

alternatives.title: Multi-leader with last-write-wins
alternatives.explanation: Cuts cross-region write latency but turns conflicts into silent overwrites. Use it only when the product can name the conflict rule and the data that may be discarded.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Write skew under snapshot isolation
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: Both sessions commit. The shared invariant is false only after both commits. Detection is a constraint query after the fact, or a 40001 abort if the transaction ran at Serializable.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Hot shard from a monotonic key
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: The newest range absorbs every insert. Cluster throughput collapses to that one node's capacity. Mitigation is a hashed or compound key, or pre-split ranges with monitoring on the tail.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Minority partition during leader election
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: The minority cannot gather a quorum, so it rejects writes. Clients retry against the majority leader. Accepting those writes would fork the log.
